newsitem.title: USA: United States takes new interest in India, Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: United States takes new interest in India, Pakistan.

text.p: Fifty years after India and Pakistan gained independence from Britain, the United States is taking a new interest in a region that some have seen as the world's most likely arena for a nuclear conflict.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright has accepted invitations to visit both countries some time this year. She will be the first holder of the office to do so since George Shultz in 1983.
Albright has a personal reason for going -- her father, Czechoslovak diplomat Josef Korbel, was an expert on Kashmir, the main bone of contention between the two neighbours.
But in general, Albright's plan reflects her interest in steering U.S. foreign policy in new directions and grappling with problems long neglected by Washington.

"We think particularly as we're entering into this 50th year of independence for both India and Pakistan that there is a reason to look at South Asia as an issue of increasing importance, increasing prominence," a senior State Department official said.
"That's going to be reflected in our relations with both India and Pakistan, as well as the other states in the region," he said.
"The absence of high-level visitors has been noticed by the people in the region, and this will reassure them of how we view them," said the official, speaking on condition he was not identified.
For much of the Cold War, Washington's relations with India and Pakistan were heavily influenced by the logic of superpower rivalry.

Ties with India, though polite, were cooled by Delhi's friendship with the Soviet Union, its leaning towards a socialist-style economy and its leading role in the Non-Aligned Movement, which Washington viewed with distrust.

Conversely, relations with India's rival Pakistan were better. In the 1980s, Pakistan served a key U.S. interest by supporting, and acting as a conduit for U.S. aid to, the Islamic guerrilla groups which waged an ultimately successful struggle to drive Soviet troops out of Afghanistan.
Events since the end of the Cold War have gone some way towards reversing that pattern.
Relations with Delhi warmed as the Soviet factor faded and India moved to free up the economy, leading the U.S. Commerce Department to designate it as a big emerging market.
Ties with Islamabad on the other hand have suffered from a series of disputes over alleged Pakistani imports of nuclear technology and ballistic missiles from China.

India and Pakistan are described by Washington as "Threshold" states that could quickly assemble a nuclear weapon if they wished, raising the stakes if they should again go to war as they have in the past over Kashmir.

Arms proliferation remains the key U.S. concern on the subcontinent, and led to a diplomatic confrontation in 1996 when the United States and its allies defeated an attempt by India to block a global nuclear test ban treaty.
But U.S. officials say this is only one element in a complex relationship with India.

The administration is also backing legislation in Congress that would restore some economic and military aid to Pakistan that has been blocked for years because of concerns over Islamabad's nuclear programme.
U.S. officials play down the fears of some analysts that Indo-Pakistani tensions could easily explode into nuclear conflict.

"I think it's a bit hyperbolic to suggest that we're going to see a nuclear exchange because of tensions between India and Pakistan," one U.S. official said. "It certainly does not ring true with the present environment between the two countries, which is as good as it's been in years."

U.S. officials make little secret of their view that the present governments in India and Pakistan are improvements on their predecessors that offer hopes of lasting peace despite continued verbal sniping.

After a three-year hiatus, the two countries in March resumed a peace dialogue focusing on Kashmir -- a mostly Moslem Himalayan region which has been divided between the two countries since shortly after their independence.

"Both of the present leaders have reached the conclusion that their long-term interest relies upon an improved relationship, and we welcome very much the structure that they have put into place to deal with that," a U.S. official said.
